The cornet is a brass instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 423.232, in the horn and brass class of lip-vibrated aerophones. It is more compact than the trumpet and its tube is mostly conical; it has piston valves, and the player's lips vibrate in the mouthpiece to set the air column going, the valves changing the pitch. The most common form is a transposing instrument in B flat, with an E flat soprano cornet and cornets in A and C also made. It is not the cornett of the Renaissance and early Baroque. Its timbre is rounder, and it is used in brass bands, concert wind bands and orchestral passages that need a soft tone, as well as in old-style jazz bands.
短號源自郵號加裝活塞閥，1820年代先使用 Stölzel 閥，1830年代巴黎: The cornet developed from the post horn with valves added: the Stölzel valve was used in the 1820s and Paris changed to the Périnet piston valve in the 1830s. The Silesian horn player Blühmel and Stölzel improved the piston valve and shared a ten-year patent; Périnet's 1838 patent became the model for the modern brass piston valve. The name comes from French corne, a horn, but it has nothing to do with the Renaissance and early Baroque cornett. Nineteenth-century French works already have separate cornet parts, and Jean-Baptiste Arban was the first famous player. Cornet and trumpet coexisted until the early twentieth century and then converged in timbre and shape as both were improved; today the cornet is used in brass bands, wind bands and orchestral repertoire that needs a soft tone.
